narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the model estimated a 63.4% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, the model judged failure more likely than success, and that prediction led to rejection; gender and race were not used as decision factors.

The strongest reason was your third-year class standing: you were in the first decile, while admitted students averaged around the sixth decile. That gap pushed the prediction most strongly toward bar failure. Your first-year standing was the second most influential factor: a second-decile position, again well below the admitted-student average near the sixth decile, added further risk. Family income was the third factor. Being from an upper-middle-income background was common among admitted students and, in your case, leaned slightly toward passing; it was weaker than the academic indicators and did not cause the denial.

To move forward, ask admissions for specific feedback, consider retaking the LSAT and strengthening your undergraduate record if possible, and seek advising on how to demonstrate improved academic readiness, such as through additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program. Address your class-rank trend directly in any future application.
